title: Employer sorting and same-firm social interaction can inflate apparent heritability of U.S. earnings
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35746, linked U.S. Census twin and earnings records
geography: United States; twins observed as adolescents in the 2000 Census and linked to earnings about 20 years later

observations.period: 2000 Census adolescence to earnings about 20 years later; paper issued September 2026

denominator.unit: twin pairs in the linked U.S. population study, approximate

earnings_heritability.unit: estimated heritability h-squared of log earnings

employer_premium_heritability.value: employer-specific pay premiums are heritable in the baseline decomposition

same_firm_social_interaction.value: the employer-premium component is mainly driven by same-sex twins who work at the same firm

adjusted_heritability.unit: percent reduction in estimated earnings heritability when siblings who work together are excluded

inequality_mechanism.value: family-linked traits, social interaction, employer sorting, and firm-specific pay are not interchangeable explanations of earnings persistence

observations.method: Extended classical twin design using linked Census and earnings data, combined with an AKM decomposition of person-specific and employer-specific pay components and a sensitivity analysis excluding siblings who work together.
observations.uncertainty: Heritability is a population-statistical parameter, not an individual destiny or immutable genetic share. The study does not establish which social mechanisms create same-firm sorting, nor does it directly observe hiring networks, discrimination, skills, or worker control.
observations.subgroup: Same-sex and opposite-sex twin pairs and siblings in the linked U.S. population; firm, occupation, sex, and social-network patterns differ across workers.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same-firm sensitivity result can reflect social interaction, shared preferences, shared constraints, employer selection, or measurement structure. Excluding co-workers reduces one source of bias but does not identify a single causal social-network mechanism.

related_sources.claim: Official NBER DOI identifies the working paper.

boundary: This record measures population-level earnings heritability and same-firm social-interaction sensitivity in linked U.S. twin data. It does not establish individual genetic destiny, a causal hiring-network mechanism, present-day mobility policy effects, or worker-level bargaining power.
